title: Diverse Engineering Teams Start After the Offer Letter
summary: A diverse team catches more problems, but only when difference reaches the decision. What the research says, plus hiring, meeting and review habits that help.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
Standup starts two minutes late. One teammate is dialing in from a noisy café, another is still switching keyboard layouts. Then the ticket comes up. The person who used to work in support says the new error message will confuse customers. Someone else notices the ticket assumes the user is already logged in, without saying so anywhere. A newer teammate asks what "the legacy flow" actually means, and it turns out two people on the team meant different things by it. Five minutes, three catches, nothing heroic. The room just wasn't five copies of the same person.

That's the case for a diverse engineering team in one scene. It's also the easy part to write about. The hard part comes after the offer letter: whether those different people get to change decisions, or just get counted.

What the research does and doesn't say

The best-known evidence comes from social psychology, and Katherine Phillips summarized it well in How Diversity Makes Us Smarter (Scientific American, 2014). In Samuel Sommers' 2006 mock-jury study, six-person juries with two Black and four white members considered more of the case facts and made fewer errors recalling them than all-white juries. The interesting part is why: the white jurors themselves got more careful in the mixed group. In another study, three-person groups working on a murder-mystery task did significantly better when they were racially diverse.

Phillips' explanation is that when people expect others to see things differently, they prepare more and assume less. She's also upfront about the cost. Diverse groups can feel less comfortable at first, with rougher conversations and less trust. In her words, people "might not like it, but the hard work can lead to better outcomes."

Two caveats keep this honest. These are lab studies on specific tasks, and they don't promise that any given team will ship faster. And "can lead to" isn't "will". What decides it is how the team works together, which is where most of your effort should go.

Hiring is the easy half

Google's Project Aristotle studied 180 of its own teams (115 engineering project teams and 65 sales pods) to work out why some were more effective than others. The researchers concluded that what really mattered was "less about who is on the team" and more about how the team worked together. Psychological safety came first of the five dynamics they found (re:Work, Understand team effectiveness).

So hiring people with different backgrounds is the start. Whether that difference reaches the product depends on a few early moments: the first week, the first code review, the first time a new person disagrees with a senior engineer in front of everyone. If the team answers with curiosity, the newcomer learns their view has a place. If it answers with defensiveness or silence, they learn to shrink. The headcount report still counts them. The product gets nothing from them.

Habits that let difference reach the decision

None of this needs a program or a budget. It needs meeting and decision habits that don't only reward whoever talks fastest:

  • Send the agenda a day early. People who think best before speaking, or who work in their second language, get time to prepare.
  • Write decisions down in a doc or an RFC and leave a day for comments. Written input counts as much as what was said in the room.
  • Ask for risks before you ask for agreement. "Where could this break?" gets more honest answers than "Everyone OK?"
  • Rotate who runs the meeting, so the same voice doesn't set the frame every week.
  • Keep decisions out of DMs. If the real call happens in a side chat, everyone else is just an audience.
  • Explain acronyms, product history and unwritten rules. A one-page team glossary saves new people weeks of guessing.

Code review works the same way. The teammate who comments least is sometimes the one reading most carefully, and there's a whole post on making room for reviewers who rarely speak up.

Hiring without cloning the team

A hiring process narrows itself without anyone meaning it to. A few common traps:

  • "Culture fit" that nobody can define beyond "feels like us". That mostly selects for familiarity. Ask a better question: what perspective, skill or habit would this person add that the team is missing?
  • Free-form interviews where every interviewer asks whatever they like. Give every candidate for a role the same core questions and score them against a rubric you wrote before the first interview. "I just liked them" gets much harder to pass off as evidence.
  • Take-home tasks with no time limit. They favor people with free evenings over people caring for kids or parents. Cap the task at a few hours and say so in the brief.
  • Interview panels drawn from one corner of the team. Mix seniority, roles and backgrounds. Candidates notice who's interviewing them, too.

Different people find different bugs

There's a plain engineering reason to care about all this. People notice what their past work trained them to notice. Someone from support reads an error message the way a confused user will. Someone who has built apps for patchy mobile networks asks why the landing page pulls 4 MB of images. Someone from ops asks about rollback before the release plan gets approved. Someone new to the domain finds the spot where the docs only pretend to be clear.

Microsoft's Inclusive Design principles say the same thing in product terms: recognize exclusion, learn from diversity, and solve for one, extend to many. Their argument is that building for people with permanent disabilities produces results that benefit everyone. You get there faster when someone in the room has lived the exclusion and isn't guessing at it.

None of this means every discussion has to slow down, or that every opinion is equally right. Teams still need standards and someone who makes the call. Diversity improves what goes into the decision. Strong teams argue with enough trust that the argument is useful, then commit once the call is made.

People copy what gets praised

Leads have extra pull here, because the team watches what gets rewarded. If praise only goes to whoever fixes the outage most visibly at 2 a.m., people learn to perform certainty. If you also thank the person whose awkward question prevented the outage, people learn that careful thinking counts. Treat mentoring, docs, accessibility fixes and thoughtful reviews as real engineering work, in performance reviews as well as in Slack, and more ways of contributing become visible.

Try this week

  • Send the agenda for your next design meeting a day early, with the one question you most want answered.
  • Open your next decision with "where could this break?" before "does everyone agree?"
  • Pick one interview question your team uses and write down what a strong answer looks like.
  • Thank someone in public for a good question, a doc or a careful review.

faqs.q: Why does diversity matter on an engineering team?
faqs.a: People with different backgrounds notice different problems: confusing error messages, slow pages on weak networks, missing rollback plans, unclear docs. Studies summarized by Katherine Phillips in Scientific American (2014) found diverse groups considered more facts and made fewer recall errors on some tasks, partly because members prepared more when they expected different views.

faqs.q: Isn't hiring people with different backgrounds enough?
faqs.a: No. Google's Project Aristotle, which studied 180 teams, found that effectiveness depended less on who was on the team and more on how members worked together, with psychological safety first among five dynamics. Different perspectives only help when the team's habits let them change decisions.

faqs.q: What is the difference between culture fit and culture add?
faqs.a: Culture fit often ends up meaning "feels like us", which selects for familiarity. Culture add asks what perspective, skill or habit a candidate would bring that the team is missing. Pair it with structured interviews: the same core questions for every candidate and a rubric written in advance.

faqs.q: How can engineering meetings be more inclusive?
faqs.a: Send the agenda a day early, write decisions down and leave time for written comments, ask where a plan could break before asking for agreement, rotate who runs the meeting, keep decisions out of private messages and explain acronyms and unwritten rules.

faqs.q: Does a diverse team move more slowly?
faqs.a: Early conversations can feel slower and less comfortable, and Phillips notes that friction openly. Teams still need standards and a clear decision owner. The payoff is better input into decisions, so the team argues usefully and then commits once the call is made.
